newsitem.title: USA: Dlr has corrected to normal mode -- Treasury's Rubin.
newsitem.headline: Dlr has corrected to normal mode -- Treasury's Rubin.

text.p: The dollar, which plummeted to post-World War II lows against the Japanese yen in the spring of 1995 and also fell on the German mark, has corrected itself, U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said Tuesday.
Rubin said that was also the consensus of other top finance officials for the Group of Seven nations who met in Berlin over the weekend.
"We all said in Berlin on Saturday that the dollar had fallen greatly against the yen and the mark and has now corrected itself," Rubin told the House Ways and Means Committee.
"In our judgment, those asymmetries have been corrected and things have come back into the normal mode," Rubin said of the dollar's recovery from the lows.
Questioned about the potential impact of the strengthened dollar on U.S. competitiveness abroad, Rubin replied that the efficiency of American business was the key to its competitiveness.
He added, "I don't believe the dollar should be used as an instrument of trade policy.
The Treasury chief further pointed to areas in which the strong dollar has been beneficial to the U.S. economy.

"A strong dollar brings us lower inflation and lower inflation brings us lower interest rates," Rubin said. "It increases confidence in dollar-dominated assets, which in turn brings us lower interest rates."
He continued, "So I think a strong dollar has actually contributed to the prosperity we've had in the last four years."
When asked about some of the reasons for the dollar's increase in recent months, Rubin said he was reluctant to comment on the market behavior in a public forum.
"My answer could set off all sorts of effects that we might not consider to be in our interests," he said.
